In some geographic locations, this type of account is known as a step account, and may provide 1% or so more interest rate than a checking account, in exchange for requiring your funds to remain in the account for 3 months so that you do not "step out" of the superior interest rate.  In general, we recommend against holding all of your emergency fund in a retirement account, such as a 401k or an IRA.  The reason is that, if you need to access these funds because of an emergency, the penalties associated with doing so usually far outweigh the benefits of having the interest bearing account.  The one exception to this rule is if you have maxed out your traditional and Roth IRA contributions for the year, and your emergency fund total has exceeded the contribution amount.  In this case, you can contribute to a traditional IRA without penalty, and withdraw from that account without penalty, provided you are less than 59.5 years of age.  Your fund balances would be invested to maximize growth and balance across types of securities, and we would recommend against any individual security representing more than 5% of the overall asset allocation.
